text: as having cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis are a heterogeneous group, with some forms appearing to respond better to treatment than others, which makes com- parison of studies difficult.5 If the condition stabilises, the dose of corticosteroid may be reduced gradually for main- tenance. Corticosteroid therapy is usually continued life- long; attempts at withdrawal should be gradual and cau- tious. Relapse or clinical deterioration may warrant an increased dose of corticosteroid, or addition of an immu- nosuppressant.8 Many other drugs have been tried in patients with cryp- togenic fibrosing alveolitis.1,5,8-11 Ciclosporin has been used adjunctively and also as a corticosteroid-sparing treatment;11 some benefit has been reported,1 but data are too limited to support its use.8,9,11 Colchicine has been sug- gested to be as effective as corticosteroids, and some con- sider it for first-line therapy or for patients refractory to corticosteroids, either alone or with immunosuppressants.8 However, studies have generally shown no evidence of survival benefit, and others do not recommend its use.9 There are reports of response to penicillamine, but control- led studies are lacking, and in view of its adverse effects, its use is generally not recommended.8,9,11 Toxicity has limited the use of chlorambucil and methotrexate,8 and there is no evidence to support the use of vincristine or mercaptopurine.11 Despite promising preliminary results, a controlled trial of interferon gamma found no significant effects on mortality compared with placebo.9 Early trials of pirfenidone have shown improvements in pulmonary function;9 further studies are underway. Acetylcysteine is also under investigation.9,12 Experimental strategies in- clude the use of relaxin, suramin, endothelin-1 inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, and gene therapy.8,9,11 In patients in whom other options fail, lung transplantation (p.1815) should be considered.1,5,8,10,11 1.
